title: Слово о пълку Игоревѣ
titleEn: The Tale of Igor's Campaign — X: The return & praise
draftNote: Part X — the poem's final movement (the 1800 edition's seventh and last paragraph): a last invocation of Boyan over a dark, disputed proverb applied to Rus' without Igor; Igor's actual return — the sun shining again, Igor back in the Russian land, maidens singing on the Danube, Igor riding to the church of the Holy Mother of God Pirogoshcha in Kiev; the lands and towns rejoicing; and the poem's closing acclamation of Igor, Vsevolod ('Buy Tur'), Igor's son Vladimir, the princes, and the druzhina, ending on Аминь.
source: Text: editio princeps — «Ироическая пѣснь о походѣ на половцовъ удѣльнаго князя Новагорода-Сѣверскаго Игоря Святославича», ed. A. I. Musin-Pushkin, Moscow, 1800 (public domain); via Russian Wikisource. 1800 orthography preserved. Prose sense-units at the edition's punctuation (no imposed verse lineation). Transliteration: scholarly Slavist romanization (ž š č c x; ě = ѣ; ŭ / ĭ = ъ / ь). Pronunciation: reconstructed late-12th-c. Old East Slavic (see slovo-audio doc); ж/ш/ц read hard by convention. Translations made fresh from the 1800 original.
about: The poem's closing movement, and the last of the 1800 print's seven paragraphs. Boyan is invoked one final time over a dark, disputed line («и ходы на») applying a proverb — a head is heavy without its shoulders, a body ill without its head — to Rus' without Igor. The tale then turns to Igor's actual homecoming: the sun, darkened by the eclipse that opened part I, shines again; Igor is back in the Russian land; maidens sing on the Danube and their voices carry to Kiev; Igor rides to the church of the Holy Mother of God Pirogoshcha; the lands and towns rejoice, singing to princes old and young. The poem closes with an acclamation — Igor, Vsevolod ('Wild Bull'), Igor's young son Vladimir, the princes and their druzhina — ending on the single word Аминь. As throughout, several lines here are genuine dark places, above all «и ходы на», where the 1800 print is kept exactly rather than adopting any modern editorial emendation. The poem survives in no manuscript (the single copy burned in 1812), so this reading claims no more certainty than the 1800 print itself supports.

sentences.t: Рекъ Боянъ и ходы на Святъславля пѣстворца стараго времени Ярославля Ольгова Коганя хоти: тяжко ти головы, кромѣ плечю; зло ти тѣлу, кромѣ головы: Руской земли безъ Игоря.
sentences.tr: Rekŭ Bojanŭ i xody na Svjatŭslavlja pěstvorca starago vremeni Jaroslavlja Olĭgova Koganja xoti: tjažko ti golovy, kromě plečju; zlo ti tělu, kromě golovy: Ruskoj zemli bezŭ Igorja.
sentences.l: Boyan said — and the goings, unto Svyatoslav's singer of the old time, of Yaroslav, of Oleg the Kagan's beloved: heavy is it, head, without the shoulders; ill is it, body, without the head: the Russian land [is so] without Igor.
sentences.i: So spoke Boyan — and so too the old sayings — of Svyatoslav's singer in Yaroslav's time, favorite of Oleg the Kagan: 'Heavy indeed is a head without its shoulders, and ill indeed a body without its head' — such, without Igor, is the Russian land.
sentences.n: The poem's final invocation of Boyan, and one of its hardest dark places, right at «и ходы на» — printed as if ordinary words ('the goings/sayings, unto...'), but many editors instead emend to a second bard's name, Ходына ('Boyan and Khodyna'), reading the line as naming two court singers of Svyatoslav. We keep the 1800 print exactly and do not adopt that emendation (per convention, a misprint or crux is noted, never silently corrected). пѣстворецъ = 'song-maker, poet' (пѣснь + творити). The chain «Ярославля Ольгова Коганя хоти» is itself disputed in how it groups — it may describe the singer just named, or point instead toward Svyatoslav as the subject to come; 'Коганя' (Kagan's) reflects a real, rare title occasionally borne by Rus' princes in period sources, though its exact bearer here is not agreed. The proverb that follows — a head without its shoulders, a body without its head — is applied to Rus' without Igor, closing the ring begun by the poem's earlier invocations of Boyan (proem, part I).

sentences.t: Солнце свѣтится на небесѣ, Игорь Князь въ Руской земли.
sentences.tr: Solnce světitsja na nebesě, Igorĭ Knjazĭ vŭ Ruskoj zemli.
sentences.l: The sun shines in the sky, Igor Prince [is] in the Russian land.
sentences.i: The sun shines in the heavens, and Prince Igor is in the land of Rus'.
sentences.n: The sun, darkened by the eclipse at the campaign's outset (part I: «Игорь възрѣ на свѣтлое солнце и видѣ отъ него тьмою вся своя воя прикрыты»), now shines freely — the poem's clearest image of restoration. свѣтится is a present reflexive (mediopassive) form, 'shines, is shining'; небесѣ is locative singular of an old -s-stem noun, небо.

sentences.i: Maidens are singing on the Danube.
sentences.n: Дѣвици (diminutive of дѣва) singing 'on the Danube' is geographically odd so far from the Don/Donets theater of the campaign, and is likely not a literal place here but the generic river of East Slavic folk lyric, as the Danube recurs this way in later folk song. Whether the poet means it literally or conventionally is not settled, and no single reading is asserted.

sentences.t: Вьются голоси чрезъ море до Кіева.
sentences.tr: Vĭjutsja golosi črezŭ more do Kieva.
sentences.l: Voices wind across the sea, as far as Kiev.
sentences.i: Their voices wind across the sea, all the way to Kiev.
sentences.n: вьются ('wind, wreathe, swirl,' reflexive of вити) pictures the singing itself traveling like a thread or a flight of birds. 'Across the sea' is not literal geography — there is no sea between the Danube and Kiev — and is best read as hyperbole for how fast and far the news of Igor's return carries, consistent with the poem's free treatment of distance elsewhere.

sentences.t: Игорь ѣдетъ по Боричеву къ Святѣй Богородици Пирогощей.
sentences.tr: Igorĭ ědetŭ po Boričevu kŭ Svjatěj Bogorodici Pirogoščej.
sentences.l: Igor rides along Borichev to the Holy Mother of God Pirogoshcha.
sentences.i: Igor rides along Borichev to the church of the Holy Mother of God Pirogoshcha.
sentences.n: Боричевъ (Borichev uvoz) was a real ascent/road linking the Dnieper landing to Kiev's upper town, named also in the Primary Chronicle. The Богородица Пирогощая ('the Mother of God, Pirogoshcha') was a real, named icon, and the church built to house it in Kiev's Podil district was consecrated in 1136 per the chronicles — one of the few places in the poem independently datable from other sources. Богородици is spelled here with и rather than the expected dative ѣ (Богородицѣ); kept as printed.

sentences.t: Страны ради, гради весели, пѣвше пѣснь старымъ Княземъ, а по томъ молодымъ.
sentences.tr: Strany radi, gradi veseli, pěvše pěsnĭ starymŭ Knjazemŭ, a po tomŭ molodymŭ.
sentences.l: The lands are glad, the towns are merry, having sung a song to the old princes, and after that to the young.
sentences.i: The countries are glad, and the towns are merry: songs have been sung for the princes of old, and now for the young.
sentences.n: ради, весели are short-form (nominal) predicate adjectives, 'are glad,' 'are merry' (compare Здрави in unit 9) — a construction modern Russian's long-form adjectives have lost. пѣвше is a past active participle, 'having sung.' «старымъ Княземъ, а по томъ молодымъ» ('to the old princes, and after them to the young') echoes, in reverse, the poem's own opening in part I — «отъ стараго Владимера до нынѣшняго Игоря» — closing a ring around the whole work.

sentences.l: To sing [is] glory to Igor, Svyatoslav's son.
sentences.i: Let songs of glory be sung to Igor, son of Svyatoslav!
sentences.n: Пѣти ('to sing') stands bare with the dative Игорю in an optative/jussive infinitive construction, 'let it be sung to Igor' — the same pattern as part I's «Пѣти было пѣсь Игореви», there with the auxiliary было. Святъславлича, apparently genitive/accusative in form, does not match the dative Игорю beside it — a small case inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept as printed rather than corrected.

sentences.l: [Glory] to Wild Bull Vsevolod, to Vladimir Igorevich.
sentences.i: Glory to Wild Bull Vsevolod, and to Vladimir Igorevich!
sentences.n: The acclamation opened by «Пѣти слава» continues across this whole sentence. «Буй туру» = 'to Wild Bull' (dat. sg. of туръ, an aurochs — Vsevolod's epithet from part I, «Буй Туръ Всеволодъ»); Всеволодѣ is an irregular dative (the expected form is Всеволоду), kept as printed. Владиміръ Игоревичъ is Igor's young son, last seen in part IX as the 'falcon-chick' left hostage in the khans' riddling exchange; he is historically recorded as later returning to Rus' after marrying a daughter of Konchak's.

sentences.t: Здрави Князи и дружина, побарая за христьяны на поганыя плъки.
sentences.tr: Zdravi Knjazi i družina, pobaraja za xristĭjany na poganyja plŭky.
sentences.l: Hale are the princes and the druzhina, contending for the Christians against the pagan hosts.
sentences.i: The princes and their retinue are hale and well, standing against pagan troops in the Christians' defense.
sentences.n: Здрави, another short-form predicate adjective (nom. pl., 'are hale, hearty' — cf. modern здравствуй), opens the poem's closing toast to princes and druzhina together. побарая is a present active participle, 'contending, doing battle for' — casting this as their ongoing role rather than a single deed. «поганыя плъки» ('the pagan hosts') is among the poem's last uses of the word плъкъ, which also opens its title and part I's opening sentence («храбрыя плъкы»).

sentences.l: To the princes, glory; and to the druzhina, Amen.
sentences.i: Glory to the princes, and to their men — Amen.
sentences.n: The poem's final line, and its only word of direct Christian liturgical address: Аминь, 'Amen,' sealing the whole work. слава carries over onto Княземъ (dative, 'glory to the princes'); in the second half Аминь stands where a second слава might be expected for дружинѣ, so the two halves are not quite parallel — that asymmetry is kept rather than smoothed into a matched pair.

glossary.богородици: Богородица — Mother of God, Theotokos (dat. sg.; spelled with и for the expected dative ѣ — see note)
glossary.боричеву: Боричевъ — Borichev [uvoz], a Kievan ascent linking the Dnieper landing to the upper town (dat. sg., after по)
glossary.боянъ: Боянъ — Boyan (nom. sg.); the legendary bard (see note)
glossary.весели: веселъ — merry, glad (short-form pred. adj., nom. pl., agreeing with 'гради')
glossary.владиміру: Владиміръ — Vladimir (dat. sg.); Vladimir Igorevich, Igor's young son (cf. part IX's 'falcon-chick')
glossary.всеволодѣ: Всеволодъ — Vsevolod (dat. sg., irregular form for the expected Всеволоду — kept as printed; see note)
glossary.вьются: вити (ся) — wind, wreathe, swirl (3pl pres. refl., 'they wind/swirl')
glossary.головы: голова — head (gen. sg.; 'кромѣ головы' = without the head; the same form recurs earlier in the line, 'тяжко ти головы')
glossary.до: до — up to, as far as (prep. + gen.)
glossary.дружина: дружина — druzhina, retinue, companions (nom. sg., collective noun, subject alongside 'Князи')
glossary.дѣвици: дѣвица — maidens (nom. pl.; diminutive of дѣва)
glossary.за: за — for, for the sake of; behind, beyond (prep.)
glossary.здрави: здравъ — hale, hearty, healthy (short-form pred. adj., nom. pl.; cf. modern здравствуй)
glossary.зло: зъло — ill, bad, evil (short-form pred. adj., neut. sg.)
glossary.игоревичу: Игоревичь — son of Igor, Igorevich (dat. sg.); patronymic of Vladimir Igorevich
glossary.коганя: каганъ — kagan, a rare princely title (possessive adj., gen. sg., 'the Kagan's'; applied here to Oleg — see note)
glossary.кромѣ: кромѣ — apart from, without, except (prep. + gen.)
glossary.кіева: Кіевъ — Kiev (gen. sg., 'as far as Kiev', after до)
glossary.молодымъ: молодый — the young (dat. pl.; substantival, 'to the young [princes]', paired with старымъ)
glossary.небесѣ: небо — sky, heaven (loc. sg.; old -s-stem noun)
glossary.ольгова: Олегъ — Oleg's (possessive adj., gen. sg., agreeing with 'хоти'); Oleg Svyatoslavich, part of a disputed genealogical chain here (see note)
glossary.пирогощей: Пирогощая — Pirogoshcha (dat. sg. fem.); epithet of a named icon of the Mother of God and the Kiev church built to house it (consecrated 1136)
glossary.плечю: плече — shoulder (gen. dual, 'кромѣ плечю' = apart from the [two] shoulders — the dual number, as elsewhere in the poem for paired body parts)
glossary.плъки: пълкъ — hosts, regiments (acc. pl., object of 'на')
glossary.побарая: побарати — contend, do battle for (pres. act. participle/converb, 'contending')
glossary.пѣвше: пѣти — having sung (past act. participle, nom. pl.)
glossary.пѣстворца: пѣстворецъ — song-maker, poet, bard (acc. sg.; пѣснь + творити)
glossary.пѣти: пѣти — to sing (infinitive; bare optative/jussive construction, 'let it be sung' — cf. part I's 'пѣти было')
glossary.ради: радъ — glad (short-form pred. adj., nom. pl., agreeing with 'страны')
glossary.руской: руськый — Russian, of Rus' (loc. sg. fem., adj.)
glossary.святъславлича: Святъславличь — Svyatoslavich, son of Svyatoslav (gen./acc. sg., as printed beside the dative 'Игорю' — a small case inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept as printed; see note)
glossary.святъславля: Святъславль — Svyatoslav's (possessive adj., acc. sg. masc., agreeing with 'пѣстворца'); Prince Svyatoslav Vsevolodovich of Kiev
glossary.старымъ: старый — the old (dat. pl.; substantival, 'to the old [princes]', paired with молодымъ)
glossary.ти: ты — indeed (dat. sg. enclitic; ethical dative in an impersonal proverbial saying, not a literal addressee)
glossary.томъ: тъ — that (loc. sg. masc./neut.; 'по томъ' = 'after that')
glossary.туру: туръ — aurochs, wild bull (dat. sg.; epithet of Vsevolod, 'Буй Туръ')
glossary.тяжко: тяжько — heavy, hard, grievous (short-form pred. adj., neut. sg., 'it is heavy')
glossary.тѣлу: тѣло — body (dat. sg.; 'зло ти тѣлу' = 'ill [is it] to the body')
glossary.ходы: ходъ — the goings, sayings (nom. pl.; obscure crux, possibly a corruption of a proper name Ходына — see note)
glossary.хоти: хоть — beloved, wife (gen. sg.; an old noun for a loved one)
glossary.христьяны: християнинъ — Christians (acc. pl.; 'за христьяны' = 'for the Christians')
glossary.ярославля: Ярославль — Yaroslav's (possessive adj., gen. sg., agreeing with 'времени'); Yaroslav the Wise (d. 1054), though the referent is disputed in this crux (see note)
